title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: P is a prime and a is a residue with 1 <= a < P. Euler looks at the sequence of residues of the geometric progression 1, a, a^2, ... modulo P (§§1-15). In modern language this is the cyclic subgroup <a> of (Z/PZ)^*.

§16 defines two kinds of residue series. A series is 'complete' if every number 1, ..., P-1 occurs in it. It is 'incomplete' if some of them are missing. In modern terms the series is complete exactly when <a> = (Z/PZ)^*.

§17 notes that a = 1 and a = P-1 always give incomplete series, since they produce only {1} and {1, -1}. This raises the question whether some a always gives a complete series.

§18 names such a 'primitive' (radix primitiva). These are primitive roots modulo P. Euler recalls that for P = 7 the primitive roots are 3 and 5. He states that their existence for every prime is a deeper question, to be settled later in the paper.

§19 (Lemma) states that the first earlier term to recur is always 1. Suppose instead that some ε = a^μ recurs as a^{μ+ν} before 1 does. Then P divides a^μ(a^ν - 1). Since P is prime and does not divide a^μ, P divides a^ν - 1. So a^ν is congruent to 1, and ν < μ+ν, meaning 1 has already recurred. This is a contradiction.

The lemma shows the sequence is purely periodic and that the order of a exists. §20 on the next page gives periodicity. §21 shows a primitive root satisfies a^{P-1} ≡ 1. §22 begins Lagrange's theorem for <a> (the order divides P-1), leading towards Fermat's little theorem.

The page is the definitional core of the paper in which Euler introduces the term 'primitive root'.
errors: §17 says a = P-1 always gives an incomplete series 'for every divisor P'. This fails for P = 3, where a = 2 = P-1 gives residues 1, 2, which is complete; 2 is a primitive root mod 3. For P = 2, a = 1 likewise gives the complete series {1}. This is a trivial oversight for small primes.
No error in the Lemma 19 argument. It tacitly uses Euclid's lemma and the earlier pigeonhole fact (§19's 'tandem recurrere debeant') that some residue must recur.

ideas.what: Classification of residue sequences of powers a^k mod P as complete or incomplete, i.e. whether a generates (Z/PZ)^*
ideas.modern_name: cyclic subgroup generated by a; generator of the multiplicative group mod p
ideas.where_published: E449, Novi Comment. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 18 (1773/4); the precursor E262 'Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta' treats the residue cycles

ideas.what: Coining of the term 'radices primitivae' and posing the problem of their existence for every prime
ideas.modern_name: primitive roots modulo p; existence theorem
ideas.usually_credited_to: Term: Euler (1774), acknowledged by Gauss. Rigorous existence proof: Gauss (1801), with Legendre's earlier attempt
ideas.where_published: E449 (this paper); Gauss, Disquisitiones §56-57 credits Euler with the term and criticizes his existence proof

ideas.what: Lemma: the first recurring residue of a^k mod P is 1, so the sequence is purely periodic
ideas.modern_name: existence of multiplicative order; pure periodicity of a^k mod p for gcd(a,p)=1
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E262, E449); implicit earlier in Fermat

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-documented page where Euler names primitive roots and proves that the order of a exists. Both points are standard in the history of number theory, and Gauss explicitly credits Euler for the term. Nothing here is new.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image; no substantive corrections. In §17, 'Quoniam vidimus...' is partly obscured by a scan line in the image but reads as transcribed.
